newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia's Negara says lending curbs flexible.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia's Negara says lending curbs flexible.

text.p: Seeking to dispel confusion over new lending curbs that have jolted the financial markets, Malaysia's central bank said on Tuesday the limits have some flexibility and can be implemented over time.
Bank Negara Deputy Governor Fong Weng Phak also said that "not many" banks have exceeded the new limits on lending to the broad property and share market sectors.

Briefing reporters on the curbs, aimed at heading off a financial crisis similar to that of neighbouring Thailand's, he said: "It is not an industry-wide issue. There were a number (of banks) but not that many."

The curbs announced on March 28 require banks and finance companies to trim their exposure to the property sector to 20 percent of total outstanding loans from nearly 30 percent now. New restrictions were also placed on financing stock purchases.

"I think people have over-reacted without understanding the measures," Fong said, referring to the stock market. The Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's key Composite Index has plummeted 6.84 percent since the limits were announced on March 28.
Malaysia's strong economic growth meant compliance can take place in a non-crisis atmosphere over time, Fong said.
"We have the luxury of time," he said.
The intention of the new limits is to gradually reallocate resources away from property, shares and consumption to the manufacturing and productive sector, he said.
About 17 percent of total loans in the banking system is for the manufacturing sector while nearly 30 percent is allocated to the property sector, according to central bank figures.
Asked if bank earnings would be squeezed by the new measures, Fong said: "It may or may not. For the banks, it's reallocating revenues from one sector to the productive and manufacturing sector."

"The spirit of the regulations is not to plug all loopholes," Fong said. "The spirit is to send a message to the country about allocating resources to the productive sector and prevent the build-up of an asset bubble."
Malaysian officials, who have been concerned about asset inflation since 1995, became alarmed when a property crash in Thailand caused a financial crisis in that country this year.
"We don't want to see anybody crashing," he said, when asked if the central bank was willing to risk a mini-crash with the new curbs in order to prevent a larger one down the road.
Fong said the Banking Act contained penalties if banks do not ultimately conform with the new limits, but the central bank would prefer to use "moral suasion" to ensure compliance.
"We think a bit of nagging is useful before it sinks in," Fong said. Banks exceeding the limits must submit compliance plans by April 15 and quarterly reports thereafter.
The curbs would remain as long as they are needed, he said.
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday the curbs may be imposed for "two, three, even four years".
Fong said banks would not be required to call in any loans or suspend lines of credit if they are over-extended now as long as they have a plan in place to reduce the exposure over time.
The lending limits have several exemptions, he explained. Owner-occupied housing loans would be exempted under the curbs aimed at dampening property speculation.
Theme parks and hotel resorts are exempt -- but not any housing project associated with them. Golf courses, on the other hand, fall under the limits.
Lending for the purchase of shares in an initial public offering (IPO) fall under the new limits, except in the case of manufacturing and infrastructure IPOs.
Employee stock option plans are also exempt.
Banks must cut their exposure to share market related loans to 15 percent of total lending.
"The spirit is very important," Foong said. "There will always be grey areas. We need to look at (the curbs) on a case-by-case basis."
